title_en: On the Words, “God Saw All That He Had Made, and Behold, It Was Very Good”
author: Severianus of Gabala
occasion: A sermon on Genesis 1:31, defending the goodness of all created things, including animals used in Scripture as images of vice, and urging the hearers to value the divine words above all pleasures.
argument: The virtues restore in us the original beauty of the image and likeness of God, while imitating the vices of irrational animals dishonors our rational freedom. Yet the animals themselves are not evil by nature; God made all things good, and Scripture itself invites us to imitate their useful qualities, such as the ant's diligence, the bee's craftsmanship, the lion's courage, and the serpent's prudence. The same animal image can signify virtue or vice depending on how Scripture applies it, so readers must carefully distinguish the meanings. The divine words are a honeycomb sweeter and more healing than literal honey, and the hearers should keep them always in the soul.

outline.move: The preacher praises the meadows of piety, explains that virtue restores the divine image, and argues that animals used as images of vice are still good by nature because God saw all things as very good.
He shows that Scripture invites imitation of useful animal qualities, such as the ant's diligence and the serpent's prudence, and distinguishes prudence from malice.
He illustrates prudent innocence with Jacob's meeting with Esau, then explains how the same image, especially the lion, can signify either virtue or vice depending on its scriptural use.
He applies the same principle to the palm and cedar, urges imitation of the bee's honey-making rather than its sting, and closes by exalting the divine words as a healing honeycomb.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Christ: "The Savior, likened to a lion and the one who commands his disciples to be wise as serpents and innocent as doves."
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Γίνεσθε φρόνιμοι, ὡς ὁ ὄφις... καὶ ἀκέραιοι ὡς αἱ περιστεραί
_unresolved_facts.fix: Christ is likened to a lion (as the one from the tribe of Judah), but the command to be "wise as serpents and innocent as doves" is addressed to "the apostles" (τοῖς ἀποστόλοις) or "you" generally, not specifically identified as a command to his disciples in the brief's formulation—the speaker presents it as general teaching

_unresolved_facts.claim: Jacob: "Quoted with 'what does he say to Esau?'"
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Τί γάρ φησι πρὸς τὸν Ἡσαύ; Εἶδόν σου τὸ πρόσωπον, ὡς εἴ τις ἴδοι πρόσωπον Θεοῦ
_unresolved_facts.fix: The formula is "Τί γάρ φησι πρὸς τὸν Ἡσαύ;" ("For what does he say to Esau?"), not "what does he say to Esau?"—the brief omits the inferential γάρ; more importantly, the voice is introduced as indirect speech about Jacob's words, not Jacob speaking directly as a quoted voice in the same way as Scripture or Christ

_unresolved_facts.claim: Christ: "Quoted with 'the Savior says to the apostles' and 'Christ the one who said'"
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: καθὼς καὶ ὁ Σωτὴρ τοῖς ἀποστόλοις φησί... μαθητὴς γίνῃ Χριστοῦ τοῦ εἰπόντος
_unresolved_facts.fix: The first formula is "καθὼς καὶ ὁ Σωτὴρ τοῖς ἀποστόλοις φησί" ("just as also the Savior says to the apostles"), not "the Savior says to the apostles"; the second is "Χριστοῦ τοῦ εἰπόντος" ("of Christ the one who said"), a genitive construction dependent on "μαθητὴς γίνῃ" ("you become a disciple of"), not an independent quotation formula

_unresolved_facts.claim: David: "Psalmist cited as a scriptural witness to the images of serpent and bee."
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: καταβοᾷ σου ∆αυῒδ κατηγορῶν καὶ λέγων· Θυμὸς αὐτοῖς κατὰ τὴν ὁμοίωσιν τοῦ ὄφεως... κατηγορεῖ σου ∆αυῒδ, λέγων· Πάντα τὰ ἔθνη ἐκύκλωσάν με, ὡσεὶ μέλισσαι κηρίον
_unresolved_facts.fix: David is cited as a scriptural witness to the image of the serpent's anger (Psalm 57:5/58:4 LXX) and the bee's sting (Psalm 117:12/118:12 LXX), not to "the images of serpent and bee" generally—he specifically witnesses the negative applications (serpent's anger, bee's sting), not the positive qualities

_unresolved_facts.claim: defending the goodness of all created things, including animals used in Scripture as images of vice
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Ταῦτα δέ μοι ἀναγκαίως παρῆκται, ἵνα μηδεὶς εἰς ὕβριν τῆς δημιουργίας ἐκλάβῃ τὰ εἰρημένα, ὡς τοῦ Θεοῦ φαῦλόν τι πεποιηκότος
_unresolved_facts.fix: The defense of created things is explicitly framed as a necessary aside ("ταῦτα δέ μοι ἀναγκαίως παρῆκται") to prevent misunderstanding, not the primary occasion—the primary occasion is the exposition of Genesis 1:31 and the exhortation to value divine words above pleasures
